book.title: Pride and Prejudice
book.author: Jane Austen
book.shelf_actual: Social comedy with a marriage plot
book.one_line_pitch: A sharp-tongued second daughter and a rich man who insults her in public spend four hundred pages discovering they were both wrong about almost everything.

resonance.core_reason: It is the rare romance where the obstacle is not circumstance but character — both leads have to become better people before they can be together, and the book makes you watch them do it.
what_it_does_to_readers: Makes them defensive about a genre they were taught to look down on
Sends them back to reread the first proposal now that they know how it ends
Ruins other romances, where the leads merely misunderstand each other
resonance.best_life_stage: Any, but it changes shape after your own first humbling
resonance.reread_value: Very high — the first read is plot, the second is Austen's irony, and the third is the parents
resonance.the_moment: The letter after the failed proposal. Elizabeth reads it twice, and so do most readers.

craft.standout_detail: Austen reports her characters' thoughts in the narrator's own voice, so praise and mockery arrive in the same sentence — readers quote the first line constantly and half of them miss that it is a joke at the neighbours' expense, not a statement of fact.
craft.unique_claim: It is the only major romance where the heroine's decisive act is changing her mind, and the book treats that as heroic rather than weak.
formal_choices: Letters carry the turning points — Darcy's letter, Lydia's note, Mrs. Gardiner's explanation
Almost no physical description; characters are built entirely from speech
The proposals are structural twins, and the second is deliberately anticlimactic
craft.difficulty_curve: The first three chapters are the hardest — once the Bennets are straight in your head, it moves quickly.

characters.name: Elizabeth Bennet
characters.why_readers_love_them: She is funny on the page rather than described as funny, and she is allowed to be badly, embarrassingly wrong without the book withdrawing its affection.
characters.signature_moment: Refusing Darcy's first proposal in terms so scathing that he leaves the room — and then reading his letter and realising she was working from Wickham's version of events.

characters.name: Mr. Darcy
characters.why_readers_love_them: Readers love that his growth happens off the page and is shown only through what he does — the Lydia business is settled before Elizabeth learns he was involved.
characters.signature_moment: Paying Wickham's debts and telling nobody.
characters.the_case_against: A strand of readers finds him insufferable rather than reserved, and argues the book lets a wealthy man buy his way out of his own behaviour.

characters.name: Mr. Bennet
characters.why_readers_love_them: The funniest character in the book on a first read and the saddest on a second — his wit is how he avoids doing anything about his family.
characters.signature_moment: Telling Elizabeth she must be a stranger to one of her parents from this day forward.
characters.the_case_against: His detachment nearly ruins all five daughters, and the book forgives him more easily than many readers do.

characters.name: Charlotte Lucas
characters.why_readers_love_them: She makes the coldly practical choice Elizabeth refuses, and the book declines to punish her for it. Readers argue about her more than about Wickham.
characters.signature_moment: Arranging her sitting room so that she sees less of her husband.
characters.the_case_against: Some readers read her as a cautionary figure rather than a clear-eyed one.

book_quotes.text: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
book_quotes.why_it_lands: The most quoted opening in English fiction, and the whole book is in it: a claim stated as universal fact that turns out to be the private wish of one neighbourhood's mothers.
book_quotes.frequency: Constant — it is the line non-readers know
book_quotes.commonly_misread: Quoted sincerely as Austen's own view. It is free indirect irony; the 'universal' truth belongs to Mrs. Bennet and her neighbours, not the narrator.

book_quotes.text: I could easily forgive his pride, if he had not mortified mine.
book_quotes.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
book_quotes.why_it_lands: Elizabeth names the book's actual subject sixty pages in, and does not realise she is describing herself.
book_quotes.frequency: Common in discussions of the title

book_quotes.text: In vain I have struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.
book_quotes.speaker: Mr. Darcy
book_quotes.why_it_lands: The most romantic sentence in the book is the opening of its worst proposal — readers quote it straight, and the scene it belongs to is a disaster.

book_quotes.text: Till this moment I never knew myself.
book_quotes.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
book_quotes.why_it_lands: Six words for the turn the entire novel is built around.

reader_voices.quote: I put off reading this for twenty years because I thought it was a book about bonnets. It is a book about being certain and wrong.
Nobody warned me the funniest character would turn out to be the most negligent parent in English literature. That reread hit differently.
The letter chapter is the best piece of construction in the book and everyone talks about the proposals instead.
Honestly it drags in the middle third and Darcy is redeemed largely by being rich. I like it, I just do not think it is the masterpiece people say.
Read it aloud with my sister over four evenings. The dialogue is written to be spoken and it is twice as funny out loud.
Charlotte Lucas did nothing wrong and I will be taking no questions.

setting.place: Rural Hertfordshire and Derbyshire, in a handful of drawing rooms, assembly halls, and gravel walks.
setting.setting_as_character: The houses are arguments: Longbourn is entailed away from the daughters, Rosings is grandeur used as a weapon, and Pemberley is the first evidence that Darcy might be worth reconsidering.
sensory_signature: The noise of a small assembly room
setting.best_reading_conditions: Winter evenings, in more than one sitting.
setting.lingering_detail: Elizabeth walking three miles alone to a sickbed and arriving with her petticoat six inches deep in mud — the entire class argument of the novel in one image.

misconceptions.belief: It is a light romance with no real stakes.
misconceptions.reality: Mr. Bennet's estate is entailed to a male cousin. If the daughters do not marry, they are destitute when he dies — the book says so in chapter seven.

misconceptions.belief: Darcy says 'You have bewitched me, body and soul.'
misconceptions.reality: That line is from the 2005 film, not the novel. Austen's Darcy gets no such speech.

misconceptions.belief: Austen writes sincerely about romantic destiny.
misconceptions.reality: She is a satirist first. The narrator mocks nearly everyone, including Elizabeth, and the marriage plot is the vehicle rather than the point.

debates.question: Is Charlotte Lucas's marriage a tragedy or a reasonable decision?
debates.side_a: It is a quiet tragedy: she trades her inner life for security and arranges her house to avoid her husband. Austen shows us the cost precisely.
debates.side_b: It is clear-eyed and the book respects it. Charlotte has no fortune and no illusions, chooses a competence over dependence, and is materially better off than she would have been.
debates.discussion_prompt: If Charlotte had refused Mr. Collins, what actually happens to her?

debates.question: Does Darcy change, or does Elizabeth simply learn more about him?
debates.side_a: He changes. His second proposal is humble where the first was entitled, and he says so himself — he was taught good principles but left to follow them in pride.
debates.side_b: The facts change, not the man. The Wickham business, Pemberley's housekeeper, and Lydia's rescue reveal a character that was there all along.

reception.initial_reception: Published anonymously in 1813 to warm but unremarkable notices; Austen called it her 'own darling child' in a letter to her sister.
reception.reputation_arc: Modest regard through the nineteenth century, sharply rising in the twentieth as critics took the domestic novel seriously, and now near-permanent residence at the top of British reader polls.
reception.generational_split: Older readers tend to arrive through the 1995 series, younger ones through the 2005 film, and the two groups picture completely different Darcys.
reception.cultural_moment: The 1995 BBC adaptation turned a canonical novel into a mass phenomenon, and most of the fandom's shared imagery dates from it.

author.name: Jane Austen
author.biography_that_colors_the_read: Austen never married, had no fortune of her own, and spent her life dependent on family arrangements — the economics her characters negotiate were her own.
author.where_it_sits_in_their_work: The most beloved of the six completed novels, though critics more often name Emma or Persuasion her best.

author_on_the_book.quote: I must confess that I think her as delightful a creature as ever appeared in print.
author_on_the_book.source: Letter to Cassandra Austen, on Elizabeth Bennet

author.reader_tension: Readers debate how much the novels critique the class system they are set in, and how much they simply operate comfortably inside it.

Ranking every adaptation, always, at the slightest provocation
running_jokes: 'It is a truth universally acknowledged that...' applied to absolutely anything
Mr. Collins as a unit of social awkwardness

before_you_start.who_its_for: Readers who like dialogue that does everything, and who enjoy watching a sharp narrator quietly undercut her characters.
before_you_start.who_bounces_off: Readers who need external plot. Almost nothing happens outdoors, and the crises are social.
content_warnings: Coerced marriage as an economic reality
A teenage girl's elopement with a much older man

audiobook.verdict: Unusually well suited to audio — the irony that readers miss on the page is unmissable when a good narrator delivers it.

wish_id_known: The entail is the engine of the plot; read chapter seven carefully
The first line is a joke
There are five sisters and you will confuse Kitty and Mary for a hundred pages, and that is fine
companion_material: An annotated edition for the money and rank details
before_you_start.commitment_point: The Netherfield ball. If you are enjoying that, you are in.

adaptations.title: Pride and Prejudice
adaptations.reader_verdict: The fandom default — six hours, and the only version with room for the whole book.

adaptations.title: Pride & Prejudice
adaptations.reader_verdict: Beautiful and heavily compressed; it invents the lines people most often misquote.

discussion_questions.question: The first line is ironic. Who exactly is being mocked, and does the book ever let that irony go?
Is Charlotte's marriage a defeat or a strategy?
Mr. Bennet is the funniest character and arguably the most culpable. Does the ending hold him accountable?
Elizabeth changes her mind after reading a letter. Is that a satisfying turning point, or a convenience?

Mr. Collins's proposal, which is funnier aloud than on the page
Lady Catherine's confrontation with Elizabeth in the garden

The Charlotte question reliably runs longest — schedule it last
